passage:
Lokesh-sir had hired Kalyani to teach Class 8 maths at his tuition centre above the Shirpur bus stand because she said she had passed her B.Com second-year exams. She hadn't. One paper was still pending, the result due in a month.
For three weeks she taught well. The children liked her. And every night she lay awake, waiting for someone to ask for her marksheet.
On Saturday, before anyone asked, she went to his desk. "Sir, I lied. I haven't cleared all my papers. Accounts is still pending. I said it because I needed this job."
Lokesh-sir put down his pen. He was quiet for a long time. "That was wrong. You'll be an assistant, not a teacher, until the result comes. Half the pay."
"Yes, sir."
She walked down the stairs feeling awful. And lighter than she had in three weeks.
On Monday he said, "Most people wait to be caught. You didn't. Come on time."

qa.q: What would Kalyani's new role be until the result came?
qa.a: Kalyani would be an assistant, not a teacher, on half the pay.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel walking down the stairs?
qa.a: Kalyani felt awful about the consequence, yet lighter than she had felt in three weeks of lying awake.

qa.q: What made Kalyani's confession earn a second chance?
qa.a: She admitted the lie herself before anyone asked for the marksheet, accepted the demotion, and did not make excuses beyond the plain reason.

qa.q: How does Lokesh-sir seem to see Kalyani after her confession?
qa.a: Lokesh-sir seems to respect her for coming forward, since he notes most people wait to be caught and still keeps her on.

grounding: A young woman confesses a lie about her exam results before being found out, accepts a demotion, and feels awful but lighter, earning respect.

passage:
On Tuesday night Olga had texted Gabriel, the café manager in Kraków, "All locked up!" She hadn't checked the back door. On Wednesday morning, the delivery man found it wide open. Nothing was taken, but Gabriel was on the phone to the landlord, frowning.
He hadn't asked her yet. He was going to look at the camera footage after lunch.
Olga stood by the coffee machine, her stomach tight. She could wait. Maybe the footage wouldn't show the door.
She took off her apron and walked to the office. "Gabriel, it was me. I didn't lock the back door. I texted that I had, but I didn't check."
He rubbed his face. "Olga. The whole stock was in there."
"I know. I'm sorry."
"You'll lose Saturday's shift. And you lock up with me for two weeks."
"Okay."
He paused. "Thank you for telling me before I found it. That matters."

qa.q: What did Olga text Gabriel on Tuesday night?
What was Olga feeling by the coffee machine?
qa.a: Olga felt anxious, with a tight stomach, torn between waiting and hoping the footage missed the door, and owning up.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference for Olga?
qa.a: Going to Gabriel before he checked the footage and saying exactly what she did, then accepting the lost shift and extra supervision.

qa.q: How does Gabriel respond to Olga coming forward early?
qa.a: Gabriel is upset about the risk to the stock and gives a consequence, but thanks her for telling him before he found it, which shows respect.

grounding: A young café worker admits a lie about locking up before her manager finds out, accepts the consequence, and earns his respect for coming forward.
